title: Shuso's Insights on Anger
speaker: Nyogen Connie Martin
summary: Nyogen Connie Martin shares their personal journey of learning to transform anger into a catalyst for growth and healing, rather than being controlled by it. Through practice and meditation, they've come to understand that anger is not something to be eliminated, but rather transformed into love and compassion when directed towards injustices and suffering. By cultivating a sense of understanding, forgiveness, and responsibility, we can develop a more mindful and compassionate relationship with our emotions, leading to greater peace and connection in the present moment.

sentences.text: Thank you all for coming and being here.
It's amazing to me to think of all the things that had to happen for all of us to be sitting here together in this room.
Think of all the things that happened in your life that brought you here, and then think about all the people who have supported you.
It's amazing we're even alive, let alone here together.
I grew up in small town Ohio, and the idea that I would end up being a shuso in a Zen Buddhist group in the Pacific Northwest is just unbelievable.
No one would have guessed.
I'm very grateful that we're all here together.
I chose anger as the major theme for practice period because it just seems to permeate everything these days, both on a personal level and on a more global level.
It's just everyone seems to be angry.
On the personal level, anger was the beginning of my practice.
I had a son who could hear but couldn't talk.
I had actually edited a book on medical ethics at a college textbook publisher I worked for, and I knew that that kind of path, taking care of a child with special needs, was not for me.
But it came about that, as Lieutenant O'Hara on the old Star Trek series used to say, "Be careful what you wish for."
My mantra became "Be careful what you wish not for: you will get it."
And 18 years later I still struggle with anger.

But through practice, and through sitting on my cushion for hours and hours and letting anger come up and feeling it go away, sometimes sitting with tears streaming down my face for the whole period, I've gradually come to have a different relationship with my anger.

Some of that change has developed gradually over the last 15 years, but a surprising amount of it has been in the last three years, when I was first for a couple of years the head of the meditation hall.
It's a job that Hannah is doing now, and I have told her that it means that if a gunman comes into the Zendo with an AR-15 rifle, she's the one who's responsible now for going and tackling them.
It's not me anymore.
I hear there's a bonus involved.
Both as Eno and as Shuso I sit along with the priests facing out towards you guys, and that has been an amazing experience for me.
It's such a feeling of caretaking that I can't do that job and have my anger bubbling up at the same time.
Both of those jobs have helped me let go of anger, because I had to be focused on the people I was trying to take care of, if that makes sense.
So I was Eno for about two years, and now Shuso.
My concern for others just didn't easily coexist with anger and with harboring ill will.
On a more public level, on a global level, anger seems to be everywhere in national and international discourse and actions, doesn't it?
It seems like there are so many wars and so many close to wars, and so many refugees trying to find homes.
The anger is unavoidable if you listen to NPR or Democracy Now or read the New York Times.
It saturates our government and people's response to the government.
It's racial divisions.

It's in our schools, where 17 students can be shot and it's still possible to buy an assault rifle off the shelf for less than seven hundred dollars, and even after Las Vegas you can still buy a bump stock that will turn that weapon into a more efficient killing machine.
I think anger is in our family and friends because people feel helpless.
A lot of people feel helpless in the face of all the anger and in the face of all that's happening.
Could we have a little more light?
I'm having trouble seeing my notes.
Not a lot, just a little.
That's great, thank you.
That's good.
So anger even dominates humor.
If you tune into a late night TV show, the sarcasm and the anger just saturates everything.
I used to watch this quite a bit because I thought they were funny, and then I just finally decided that this isn't funny at all, and I try to avoid those now.

Anger on the public global stage also has the potential to be totally disastrous, as when our unstable president, our unstable leader, throws taunts at another country's unstable leader, both of whom have access to nuclear codes.
It's pretty scary.
It actually doesn't matter whose button is larger, because if one of them gets pushed, well, we don't know exactly what would happen.
You can probably hear that some of that anger is still in my voice as I talk about this stuff.
For one thing it's scary, and for another I feel helpless to do anything about it.
So, anger is many different things.
It can be a minor irritation because [unclear: "apparently ran out just as what"] someone was preparing for a talk.
You can guess who that happened to recently.
It can be a more serious disagreement with a friend that destroys the friendship.

I've spoken before about the problems I experienced with my sister when our mother died, and it turned out within an hour or so, or even less, Jeannie was telling me all about how angry she was at me for all these different things that I had done over the years.
Some of the things I had done, but some of what she was talking about were stories that she had made up herself about what she thought I thought of her, and she was wrong.
I always looked up to my big sister.
Anger can take over our bodies and minds.
For me it sometimes led to serious depression, and there's one particular teaching that has helped me a lot in facing anger and in dealing with depression.
That's Shanti Deva, the opening lines of the Dhammapada, the Bodhicharyavatara.
Oh, I knew I shouldn't try to say this word, Bodhi charia.
Would someone say it for me?
Yeah, thank you.
I found this translation on the everyday zen website a long, long time ago, and I've had a copy of it on my refrigerator for years.
If you were in the class and you want to say this with me because you remember it, that would be great.
You're welcome to recite it with me, please, though let me set the pace.
*What we are today comes from our thoughts of yesterday, and our present thoughts build our life of tomorrow.
Our life is the creation of our mind.
If a person speaks or acts with an impure mind, suffering follows as the wheel of the cart follows the beast that pulls it.
What we are today comes from our thoughts of yesterday, and our present thoughts build our life of tomorrow.
If a person speaks or acts with a pure, pure mind, joy follows as the shadow follows the body.*
*He insulted me, he hurt me, he defeated me, he robbed me.
Those who think such thoughts will not be free from hate.
For hate is not conquered by hate.
Hate is conquered by love.
This is the eternal law.*
At first I loved this.
At first it seemed ridiculous to me, but it also intrigued me.
How could it be true?
My mind doesn't create what happens in my life, or does it?
What happens if I speak or act with an impure mind, a mind that arises from anger and fear, a mind that clings to me and mine and says "I, I, I"?
There is me, and then there is everything else that is not me.

But what happens if I speak and act with a pure mind, a mind that recognizes impermanence and emptiness, a mind that sees clearly that everything is connected, everything is intertwined with everything else in a dance that will continue throughout space and time?
The last verse in this quote was especially significant.
In fact it was heart piercing to me when I went through a divorce that I didn't want.
Those words, "he defeated me, he hurt me, he robbed me": oh, did I think those thoughts.
They were true, they were absolute.
He did that, that's what happened.
He hurt me, he betrayed me.
And that brings me back again to that first dokusan with Norman where I said that I didn't want to live my life in anger, and then those last lines: "For hate is not conquered by hate.
Hate is conquered by love.
This is the eternal law."
So if we can drop the hate and blame, what is left?
What would still be there?
It seems to me that there would still be energy, and if we can somehow retain the energy of anger, can we transform it and make use of it?
Can there really be righteous anger?
I think there can be.
But not just that there can be, but that there must be righteous anger.
How can anyone not feel righteous anger in the face of the pain felt by all the family and friends of those school kids who were shot, and the teachers who were shot, in Florida?
Think of their parents, their brothers and sisters, their cousins, aunts and uncles, friends.
And as those children have come out and spoken in protest to the government, how can we not join in their righteous anger, even as many of our politicians continue to accept money from the NRA?
It's maybe too easy, or too heartbreaking, to focus just on the children that these things happen to.
Don't forget the people gunned down at the Route 91 Harvest country music festival in Las Vegas: 58 people dead and 851 injured, 10 minutes and 1100 rounds fired.
Climate change: I think there's a question of whether our species will become extinct as the earth heats up and rebels against our mistreatment of our home.
How can we not feel righteous anger as politicians ignore that change that is already killing people and animals around the world?
Why is this not headline news every day?
How can we not feel righteous anger at the genocide that has been happening in Myanmar, over a thousand deaths, mass graves found, according to CBS online news?
It has been a systematic slaughter by the military with help from Buddhist neighbors.
I'm sorry to be so depressing about this, but I think we have to look at what our life really is.
It seems to me that if we do not allow righteous anger, then whatever is happening in the world is what is happening, with no hope of changing it and no hope of the world becoming a better place.
But I think it can change, and I think the world can become a better place.
The school kids who have been speaking out really are an inspiration for me.
It's difficult to separate an action from the person behind the action.
I find this very difficult to do.
I sort of want to look at a situation and place blame: this person is at fault for this, this is why this happened.
But that is not the understanding of our practice.

Our practice is rooted in finding that understanding and finding forgiveness, and it's really been only recently that I have seen that the people I want to blame have themselves been part of the same uprising of this world, the same manifestation, as I have been and you have been.
It's the world that comes up moment by moment.
This understanding has been slow to come for me, and it's still a little shaky.

I think the key to finding that understanding and forgiveness is in recognizing the incredible complexity of our lives, and in understanding that we have very limited control in directing ourselves, our lives, or the lives of the people around us.
Then consider what brought the person that you might see as an enemy to where they are, to the same point in their, in his or her life.
So how much control did that person have over the present moment?
A child can be taught that money is everything.
Still, there's that next decision, that next step, and we do have a moment to decide how to act, and that moment of decision is there for all of us.
I've focused quite a bit on a teaching of Norman's that says that I am not at fault for the current condition of the world.
You are not at fault for the current condition of the world.
However, I am responsible, as you are, for what comes next.
I'm responsible for the choice I make in that current moment.
So I'm not at fault for everything that's come up now, that's the result of such complexity and so many different things that have happened, that no one is in control of.
But we all are individually in control of what we do in the next moment.
I believe everyone has the same responsibility to respond to the present moment with integrity and compassion.
It's important that it be a response and not a reaction, because if it's just a reaction, it will come out of our anger.
If it's a response, then it has a chance to do some good in the world.

I sometimes struggle with forgiveness, for others and for myself, because there is that next present moment when we all have to make a decision of how to act, and it's awfully easy for judgment to come up, and to be judgmental about my own actions and other people's.
So that's something I'm still working on.
I think all of us are.
If we practice anger, we will get very good at it.
We watched a video of a young boy telling us about that.
So if we practice anger, we will become very good at being angry.
On the other hand, we can practice forgiveness, and just by practicing it we can become really good at it.
We can also practice gratitude, and just by practicing it we can nourish it and find hope.
I'd like to suggest that you try a practice that Steve Stuckey used to do.
He is a former abbot of San Francisco Zen Center, and he recommended that when you get out of bed in the morning, just as your feet hit the floor, let the word gratitude rise up in your mind.
I have a new morning practice myself.
From my bed, even before I get up, I can look through my bedroom into a bathroom that now has a cover of a calligraphy.
It's huge, six feet tall and four feet wide, and what it says is "Every day is a good day."
The artwork has only been out for a couple of weeks, but it's already had a real impact on how I start my day, just thinking that thought: every day is a good day.
It's like how I came to appreciate those opening lines of the Dhammapada.
At first I was dubious: wait a minute, every day is not a good day.
But if you look at a larger level that includes everything, every day is a good day, no matter what happens or what the day brings forth.
So thank you, Tim.
All of the precepts can be understood on multiple levels.
The ninth precept tells us, do not harbor ill will.
So what does that mean?
If we look at a literal level, "just don't be angry" seems pretty clear, but also pretty impossible.
When I was going through my divorce with Ford, I was deeply angry.
I always said the lines from the Dhammapada that I really related to.
But sitting many, many hours of zazen and reading Shantideva's verses many, many times has helped me let go of those kleshas, those afflictive emotions, as they're called.
Those emotions, I realized, have almost nothing to do with Ford.
They're what's inside myself, and they reflect my relationship with the world.
I know I'm repeating myself here, but it's so important.

When that anger arises again, which it will, I can remind myself: *hate is not conquered by hate; hate is conquered by love; this is the eternal law.* And as painful as it is, I can still also remember the deep love that I once had for Ford.
He's a good person, he's a good father most of the time.
This precept doesn't say never be angry.
It just tells us to let it go, not to hold on to it, not to harbor it or nourish it.
And then on the compassionate level, do not harbor ill will: my understanding and my compassion must extend to everyone.
Chris has emphasized that many times, and I've learned from her.
No one would choose to have a black soul filled with hatred and built on fear.
I think that those who have a deep hatred and contempt for others must have those same feelings toward themselves.
They must experience an almost absolute loneliness, even if they don't recognize it.
They really are to be looked at with compassion.
And then on the ultimate level, do not harbor ill will.
Maybe this is the compassionate level just extended into the absolute.
There's a NASA photo of the earth.

I don't know what website I spotted this on, and I've looked and looked for it and I can't find it again, but it's an image of the universe, and there's this little tiny speck, this little tiny dot, that is labeled Earth.
To me it's a picture of impermanence and emptiness.
We are a very, very small, very tiny part of this universe, and I hope we can all treasure our lives and the lives of others.
It is rather daunting, but I think we can develop an unflinching willingness to look closely at our lives, to experience impermanence, maybe even to experience emptiness, without fear.
My life for a long, long time was turning away from things that were painful.
I think I learned that from my mother: just don't deal with it, just look the other way, turn the other way and it won't hurt so much.
To turn toward anger is difficult.
But I want to see my life as it really is, even if that sometimes seems terrifying, because absolutely everything is connection.
Everything is in relationship to something else or someone else, and everything and everyone depends on everything and everyone else.

As part of the practice period class on anger, I asked each participant to choose a stone or a rock to carry with them, in a pocket, or to put on an altar or on a window sill, and keep it as a reminder to pay attention to the anger arising every day in our lives, multiple times.
Some of the rocks came from the beach at Sandy Point, and I gathered them up and polished them.
Some came from, well, there were some agates that came from the Oregon coast, the sea lion caves gift shop, about 40 years ago.
The agates are incredible.
They're polished rocks that you can actually see through.
You hold an agate out and put a finger across the back of the rock, and you can see the shadow move.
I'd like to suggest that each of you here today do something similar: find a stone or a rock and carry it in your pocket, or put it on your altar or on the window ledge above the sink.
It can still be a reminder of anger if you want it to be, if that is what you need to work with and the rock helps.
You can still use it that way.

But you can also take a different view of it, a different perspective, and let the rock be a reminder of the beauty of this world and the intimate connection and interbeing we have with this planet, with all of its people, its creations and its insentient beings: the rocks, the waterfalls, the red cedars, the snow on the mountain peaks, clouds in the blue sky.
I have started to wonder if there actually are any insentient beings.
I don't think there are.
I think that the trees and the rocks just live their lives at a slower pace than we do.
We know that trees can communicate with each other.
If a disease strikes this tree in one part of the forest, trees on the other side of the forest, miles away, may put out a defensive toxin against whatever bug is attacking the forest.
How did they know to do that?
So we know that trees can communicate with each other, but I wonder what rocks might have to say if we could hear them.
The waterfalls and clouds are never still, and I think they possibly live their lives completely, and live and die in each moment.
That's what we all do, in some ways.
I'm going to let the rock on my altar remind me of a day a couple weeks ago when it was snowing and I let my dog off.

Usually I keep my dog on his leash because I'm afraid he'll run into the street or something, but there was no traffic, and I let him off his leash and he just ran around that yard playing in the snow with such gay abandon.
He's probably about 10 or 11 years old, but he was acting like he was two or three, and I was just laughing out loud because he was having so much fun.
I want all of us to have that experience of freedom and joy in our lives that Angus had on that snowy day.
There's a poem by Wendell Berry that I'd like to read to close off.
Kate McCandless found this a long time ago and didn't mind at all if I stole it from her, and I think it still resonates strongly in today's world.

It also reminds me of an exercise that we did in our anger class, where each person held their anger and took it to a still pond in the forest where an animal came forth and took the anger away from them.
Mine was a great blue heron.
So anyway, the poem is called "The Peace of Wild Things."

*When despair for the world grows in me, and I wake in the night at the least sound in fear of what my life and my children's lives may be, I go and lie down where the wood drake rests his beauty on the water, and the great blue heron feeds.
I come into the peace of wild things who do not tax their lives with the forethought of grief.
I come into the presence of still water, and I feel above me the day-blind stars waiting with their light.
For a time I rest in the grace of the world, and I'm free.*
I'll read this once more.

*When despair for the world grows in me, and I wake in the night at the least sound in fear of what my life and my children's lives may be, I go and lie down where the wood drake rests his beauty on the water, and the great blue heron feeds.
I come into the peace of wild things who do not tax their lives with forethought of grief.
I come into the presence of still water.
I feel above me the day blind stars waiting with their light.
For a time I rest in the grace of the world, and I'm free.*
So I do, in spite of all the negative news that we can find, I do believe that we can find peace and reconciliation with other people.
In the meantime it's just so important to appreciate everything about this world that there is.
I don't know if it's partly because I'm getting older or exactly why, but I've started noticing more and more just a spot, a splash of beauty in something that almost stops my heart.
I took Angus out for his pee and poop walk the other day, and there was a deer in my yard.
It wasn't scared, it didn't run away, but it was just a sudden appearance of incredible beauty.
There's also a tree, an old cedar tree, that I pass when I take a walk, and the colors in the bark are incredible.
There's brown and green and gray, and for some reason there are some streaks that look almost purple.
It's just so amazingly beautiful.
And being shuso, I've also found more connection with people in the sangha.
People I would say hello to before, we got together for tea and got to know each other a bit, and I look forward to some of those connections becoming more friendships.
That was a really lovely thing to happen.
So thank you all for listening, and I wish everyone well.
Many gassho.
